newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Koor eyes Egypt privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Koor eyes Egypt privatisation.

text.p: Israel's Koor Industries Ltd President Benjamin Gaon will soon go to Egypt to investigate the possiblity of buying into privatisation of telecommunications and cement companies there, an Israeli newspaper said on Monday.
Koor spokesmen were not immediately available to comment.

The news broke a day after the Arab League, meeting in Cairo, passed a resolution calling on member states to suspend steps toward normal relations with Israel and to reactivate the Arab boycott against it over its breaking ground for a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem this month.
It was not clear how the Arab League decision might affect Gaon's plans.
The Haaretz daily said Gaon told it in an interview that Koor hoped to participate in Egyptian privatisation together with Egyptian partners, possibly the Kato group.
Haaretz said Gaon would visit Egypt within the next several weeks as the guest of Kato Chairman Ibrahim Kamel, who earlier this year bought a small stake in Koor.
Kamel in February called the investment symbolic, a political gesture to promote peace. It was the first investment by his companies in an Israeli company.
It said Gaon would bring a delegation of top executives of Koor companies with him on the trip.
Kamel visited Israel in January as Gaon's guest. During the trip he met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Earlier this month, a Koor source speaking on condition of anonymity said the concern was negotiating with four foreign companies for the sale of a 20 percent stake of Nesher Cement, which is controlled by Mashav Initiating and Development Ltd, a joint venture of Koor and Clal Israel.
Mashav has been seeking a partner for more than a year as a means of breaking into the Middle East market. In Israel it has a monopoly on cement production.
The companies Koor was negotiating with were France's Lafarge, Mexico's Cemex, Italy's Italcementi, and Switzerland's Holderbank.

Arab foreign ministers meeting in Cairo agreed to recommend that their countries suspend normal relations with the Jewish state, close down any Israeli missions, reactivate the boycott and withdraw from multilateral Middle East talks.
But Egypt and Jordan, the two states which could have the greatest impact, appeared to be exempt from action because they have signed binding peace treaties with Israel.

The resolution is more pertinent to other Arab countries such as Morocco, Tunisia, Oman and Qatar which have made tentative gestures towards Israel since it reached its first agreement with the Palestinians three and a half years ago.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said it was up to individual countries how they put into practice the resolutions, which also remain subject to approval by their heads of state and government.
